My dad and I really wanna do Half Dome at Yosemite, but we're hiking noobs. Do you guys have any links I could check out or advice to give to find fitting hiking boots? Your experiences?

I've hiked halfdome twice and I would recommend getting a solid hiking boot. Both time I went is was rocking a pair of Asolo fsn95. They performed excedingly well. I currently wear Alico boots and am Also very happy with them. I'll wear Asics trail runners sometimes on shorter dayhikes. Also, make sure this isn't your first hike. Find someplace nearby and load up a daypack and hit some shorter trails in your new boots to break them in before trying to conquer a tougher trail like halfdome. Where do you hail from? I could maybe make some suggestions on some preliminary trails to break in those new boots.

Awesome thank you. Why were your Asolos so good? Did they help in water or good hold or something? I'm asking bc I'm not sure what makes a good hiking shoe. It might be different for different people. Also, I hail from southern AZ.

I really liked the Asolos. They did take some time to break in, about 3-4 days(I just wore them to work daily) but they proved to be very comfortable. Definitely waterproof, I really like to be able to just slosh through puddles on the trail instead of trying to avoid them. The soles had excellent tread pattern and great grip. I've hiked a lot of different terrain and always felt confident in my footing. I wore these boots until the soles were worn smooth. I wore them on every hiking and backpacking trip and most days as a work boot for 2 maybe 2 1/2 years. All in all, a great boot, they gave me hundreds of trail miles and held up really well throughout.
Of course, different people like different things. Some peoples feet are different than others and so a different shoe or boot works better for them. Some other things to consider would be where you'll be using them the most and pick something that is geared towards that environment. If you often encounter water and stream crossings in your trips with a lot of uneven and rugged terrain the Asolos would probably be a good boot for you. But, being that you're from the southwest(I'm under the Impression it's pretty hot, dry and mostly sandstone) you may benefit from having something less waterproof and more ventilated.

Well, I don't know anything about Yosemite, but I do know a bit about boots:

Hiking boots have to be as comfortable as needed. I mean that you can hike strenuous trails with just a pair of jogging shoes, as long as you've trained for that. Your foot consists in large part of a lot of small bones and muscles, and you can train them to be comfortable with climbing over big rocks with heavy gear and only a pair of sneakers or flip-flops.

Of course there are limits to this, such as the need for a higher boot for wet conditions, gore-tex membrane against relentless moisture, or stiff, crampon-ready soles. Here are some tips for what questions you can try to answer about your gear:

  • In what conditions will I use them? Wet/dry, hot/cold, flat/rocky trail etc.
  • How trained are my feet? The more you train, the likelier you are to finish a trail with more flexible shoes. Also, use your shoes before your trip, so you'll easily learn how you can adjust them, and if there are pressure-points. It'll save a lot of discomfort.
  • Do I need merino-wool socks? Your feet sweat, and a lot when hiking. If it's hot, they'll sweat more, so if you're going to hike in mostly dry, hot weather, you can definitely refrain from a gore-tex membrane. That'll only make your shoes more expensive and unnecessarily toasty. Plus, when wet, gore-tex doesn't dry as quickly as a shoe without it. Merino wool helps wick sweat away from your skin, and it retains a lot of warmth when wet. So if you'll be hiking in the snow, and your shoes get soaked (even with gore-tex it happens), your wet woolen socks will still hold a lot of body-heat.
  • Do I need gore-tex? See above
  • Do I need a high boot? A higher boot only serves against external moisture. NOT for stabilizing your ankle. It's a myth, and quite a persistent one. A higher boot also weighs more, so your hike will eventually cost more energy and require more stamina.

When fitting, put your heel firmly to the back, and tighten the boot. Now you'll stand, and smack the front tip against the ground or a wall. If your toes quite firmly touch the front, they're too small. Probably you'll end up buying 1-2 sizes too big for normal shoes. I have a pair of Lundhags, and while I normally wear a US size 11, now I've got a size 12.

One last tip, and it's an important one: before you'll start fitting shoes, go for about an hour walk. Your feet'll swell up a bit, and they'll resemble your hiking physique better than when well-rested.
